"Farida, sit down. Read this paragraph aloud for me."

"Professor Mridul, I—"

"Please."

"'The novel critiques colonial railway policy in the seventh chapter.'"

"There is no railway in the seventh chapter, and the book has no colonial chapter at all. Also, this quote does not appear anywhere in the text."

Farida's face went hot. "I ran out of time. I put the question into a tool and submitted what it gave me."

"The college rules say your submission must be your own work. You will need to write it again, with a note to the committee. You'll also lose the marks for this one."

"I know. I'm sorry. I didn't learn anything, did I?"

"Not from that one."

qa.q: What did the professor say was missing from the seventh chapter?
qa.a: There is no railway in the seventh chapter.

qa.q: What is Farida feeling as Farida's face goes hot?
qa.a: Farida feels embarrassed and regretful, having taken a shortcut under time pressure that has now cost marks.

qa.q: What could Farida do next time when short of time, and why?
qa.a: Farida could ask the professor for a short extension or submit a smaller honest draft, because an honest partial attempt teaches more than a polished copy.

qa.q: How might Professor Mridul see the submitted essay?
qa.a: Professor Mridul sees work with invented quotes that does not show what Farida understands, and is bound by the rules on originality.

grounding: Pressed for time, a student submits an AI-written essay unchanged, and the errors, policy breach and lack of learning cost more later.

I still remember the night: three assignments due, one essay left, and it was past one. I pasted the question into the chatbot, copied the answer into the template, typed my name, and submitted. I didn't even read it through.
Two weeks later, the course coordinator called me in. The essay quoted a book chapter that doesn't exist and gave the wrong year for the policy it was meant to discuss. It had also been flagged under the university's originality rules. I sat there going red while my friend Usha waited outside.
I had to rewrite it, lost most of the marks, and got a warning on my record. The worst part came at the end-term exam. The same topic came up, and I had nothing to say, because I'd never actually learnt it.
That shortcut saved Alka one night and cost Alka the whole term.

qa.q: What mistakes did the coordinator find in the essay?
qa.a: It quoted a book chapter that doesn't exist and gave the wrong year for the policy it was meant to discuss.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel in the coordinator's office?
qa.a: The narrator felt ashamed and exposed, sitting there going red while Usha waited outside.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were in that position on the night of the deadline?
qa.a: I would ask for a short extension or submit a rough draft of my own, because a weaker honest essay costs less than a warning and an empty exam answer.

qa.q: How might Usha see what happened, waiting outside?
qa.a: Usha probably felt worried for a friend, not knowing how bad the meeting was, and may have been careful about Usha's own shortcuts afterwards.

grounding: Shows a student under time pressure submitting an unchanged tool-written essay that has errors, breaks the originality policy and leaves nothing learnt.

Writing centre note, Thursday. Tutor: Rajni.
Preeti came in today after her history essay was returned with a flag under the college originality policy. She said she had been working evening shifts at the bakery all week and had pasted the prompt into a chatbot the night before it was due, then submitted it as it came.
She showed me the marked copy. The lecturer had circled two quotations with no source and a date that was off by fifty years. Preeti kept folding and unfolding the corner of the page and said, "I didn't even read it. I don't know what it says."
What I did next: we read the essay aloud together and she listed what she actually knew about the topic, which was more than she expected. We booked two more sessions to rebuild it in her own words, and I sent her the form for requesting a resubmission.

qa.q: Where had Preeti been working in the evenings that week?
qa.a: She had been working evening shifts at the bakery.

qa.q: What does Preeti's folding of the page corner suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she is anxious and ashamed, especially as she admits she never read the essay she submitted.

qa.q: What else could Preeti have tried on the night before the deadline?
qa.a: She could have written a short, rough version of what she already knew and asked for extra time, since that knowledge turned out to be more than she expected.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Rajni, the tutor?
qa.a: Rajni sees a tired student who knows more than her essay showed, and treats the problem as something to rebuild rather than only punish.

grounding: Shows the cost of a student submitting a tool-written essay unchanged: errors, an originality-policy flag and no learning, followed by a support plan.
